summary:
We built a health monitoring app, which includes; vitals tracking, including but not limited to heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, cabin data, such as pressure, temperature, sleep and mood data, exercise, bone and muscle density data, and radiation data, including total career radiation exposure. 

We also added Bluetooth connectivity, testing this with a Garmin which gave live heart rate, and SpO2 readings, which were shown as live charts, and integrated a camera system to detect heart rate through the shift in colour in a human face as blood is pumped through this face. 

This creates a health tracking tool that includes all vital extra-terrestrial parameters which could impact an astronauts health and quality of life, using Python. This enables longer stay in space and human extra-terrestrial travel.
details:
What it does and how it works

Astronaut Health Monitor is a dashboard that tracks crew health on a long-duration mission and flags problems before they become emergencies. It follows about 30 health and environment parameters for each crew member and for the cabin, grouped under NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile/closed environments.

Every reading is compared with a published limit and shown as green (in range), yellow (watch) or red (alert). A crew overview shows each astronaut’s overall status at a glance, an alerts list shows everything out of range and why, and each parameter has a chart with its safe band drawn behind it. A mission clock lets you replay the mission or jump to key events such as a solar particle event, a CO2 scrubber fault or a crew illness.

Each value comes from one of three sources, and the dashboard labels which: live readings from connected trackers, real records measured on the International Space Station, or simulation. [Cabin temperature, humidity, CO2 and radiation dose come from real ISS records published in NASA’s Open Science Data Repository Environmental Data Application.] [A Bluetooth heart-rate tracker feeds a crew member’s live heart rate.] [A webcam measures fatigue from eye closure and estimates heart rate without contact.] Individual astronaut vitals are not public, so those are simulated around realistic baselines.

Benefits and intended impact

On a mission to the Moon or Mars, communication delays mean the crew cannot rely on flight surgeons on Earth to spot every problem in real time. Our tool puts all the health information in one place, applies NASA’s own limits automatically, and tells the crew what needs attention first. The same approach could support remote medicine on Earth, for example at polar stations or on ships.

Tools and data

Python, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas and NumPy for the dashboard; OpenCV and MediaPipe for the camera; Bleak for Bluetooth trackers. Limits come from NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2 and NASA OCHMO technical briefs, with the NHS NEWS2 early-warning score for vital signs. Background came from NASA Human Research Program pages on hazards and risks and the Canadian Space Agency’s work on neutron radiation monitoring.

Creativity

We organised the dashboard around NASA’s five hazards instead of a flat list of numbers, so every reading is tied to the risk it relates to. Yellow bands are our own early-warning margin ahead of NASA’s hard limits, giving the crew time to act. Any device can be connected through a simple shared interface, so the system grows with whatever sensors a mission carries.

What we considered

Honesty about data: every value is labelled live, real or simulated. Accessibility: status is shown with an icon and a word as well as colour. Credibility: every limit has a cited source, and we note where a band is our own choice. Practicality: thresholds live in one editable file, so limits can change without touching code.
